version.changelog: v1.0.3 — consistent naming: all paths, credentials, and references now use imap-smtp-mail

vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: imap-smtp-mail
Version: 1.0.3

The imap-smtp-mail skill is a well-structured tool for email management that includes robust security controls. It implements file access whitelisting via ALLOWED_READ_DIRS and ALLOWED_WRITE_DIRS in scripts/imap.js and scripts/smtp.js to prevent unauthorized file operations, and enforces an approval-based workflow for sending emails. While scripts/email-watch-lite.js uses execFileSync to invoke the OpenClaw CLI for automated inbox monitoring, this behavior is clearly documented and aligned with the skill's stated purpose of providing an optional background watcher.

llm.summary: The skill's code and runtime instructions match an IMAP/SMTP email tool, but registry metadata omits the sensitive environment variables it requires and the skill's runtime can invoke the OpenClaw CLI — these mismatches warrant caution.

dimensions.detail: The scripts (imap.js, smtp.js, email-watch-lite.js) implement IMAP/SMTP mailbox access, attachment parsing, and sending — this matches the skill description. However the registry metadata declares no required environment variables or primary credential even though the SKILL.md and scripts expect an on-disk credentials file with IMAP/SMTP credentials (IMAP_USER, IMAP_PASS, SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASS, etc.). That metadata omission is an incoherence.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Runtime instructions require creating ~/.openclaw/credentials/imap-smtp-mail.env (or setting EMAIL_ENV_FILE). The scripts read that file (dotenv), read/write workspace files (contacts, attachments) but enforce ALLOWED_READ_DIRS/ALLOWED_WRITE_DIRS. The watcher (email-watch-lite.js) may run the local OpenClaw CLI to send alerts/agent messages; this is documented in SKILL.md, so behavior is in-scope but it can cause outbound agent activity and will run the OpenClaw CLI with the process environment (which includes loaded env secrets).
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no remote download/install step in the registry; package.json lists normal npm dependencies and SKILL.md instructs running npm install in the skill folder. That is standard and proportionate for a Node-based tool.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill requires highly sensitive credentials (IMAP_USER/PASS and SMTP_USER/PASS) and other environment settings, but the registry metadata lists 'Required env vars: none' and 'Primary credential: none' — an inconsistency. The code also loads the entire process.env into child exec calls (execFileSync openclaw, env: process.env), so secrets present in the environment would be visible to any invoked local CLI. The number and sensitivity of env vars is expected for an email tool, but they should have been declared in metadata and documented clearly to the installer.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request always:true and does not try to modify other skills or system-wide settings. The setup script writes a credentials file under ~/.openclaw/credentials (normal for this use). Note: the watcher can be run to trigger outbound agent messages via the OpenClaw CLI; autonomous invocation is allowed by platform defaults but is not granted here by 'always'.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill appears to implement a legitimate IMAP/SMTP client, but there are a few things to check before installing: 1) The registry metadata does not list the sensitive environment variables this code actually needs — expect to provide IMAP_USER/IMAP_PASS and SMTP_USER/SMTP_PASS in the credentials file (~/.openclaw/credentials/imap-smtp-mail.env). 2) The watcher can call the local OpenClaw CLI with the process environment; any secrets present in process.env would be available to that child process. 3) Prefer using app-specific passwords (e.g., Gmail app password) or a dedicated mailbox, and set file permissions (setup.sh already sets 600) and ALLOWED_READ_DIRS/ALLOWED_WRITE_DIRS as restrictive whitelists. 4) If you don't fully trust the publisher, review the scripts locally (they are included) and run in an isolated environment (container/VM) before supplying real credentials. 5) Consider whether you want the inbox-watcher behavior (automated agent triggers) — if not, avoid running email-watch-lite or remove/disable it.
